title: Allergen awareness
siteNotes: Where the allergen matrix or allergen information is kept, and how it is kept up to date
Who the allergen lead (or the manager responsible for allergen questions) is on each shift
How an allergy order is flagged on the till, ticket or pass at this venue
Where the venue's allergen-safe utensils, boards and prep area are, if it has them
Where the nearest adrenaline auto-injector held by the venue is, if any, and who is trained to help
The notice that tells guests to ask staff about allergens, and where it is displayed
How pre-packed-for-direct-sale (PPDS) items, if any, are labelled here
legalNotes: The 14 allergens: Food Information Regulations 2014 (SI 2014/1855), adopting Regulation (EU) 1169/2011 Annex II. List matches FSA guidance: celery, cereals containing gluten (wheat, rye, barley, oats), crustaceans, eggs, fish, lupin, milk, molluscs, mustard, peanuts, sesame, soybeans, sulphur dioxide and sulphites (at more than 10 mg per kg or per litre), tree nuts (almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, brazil nuts, cashews, pecans, pistachios, macadamia or Queensland nuts). https://www.food.gov.uk/safety-hygiene/food-allergy-and-intolerance

Non-prepacked food: allergen information must be available for every dish and can be given in writing or orally, with a clear sign telling guests how to ask. Oral information must be backed by written information that is easy to find. Source: Food Information Regulations 2014 and FSA allergen guidance for food businesses. Verified in outline; the full guidance pages could not be fetched, so the venue should check its method against FSA guidance.

PPDS (prepacked for direct sale) food must carry a full ingredients list with allergens emphasised on the label. Natasha's Law: Food Information (Amendment) (England) Regulations 2019, in force 1 October 2021. Verified (date given in the venue's own course index; consistent with FSA guidance).

Cross-contact: FSA allergen guidance explains it as an allergen getting into food that does not contain it, through shared utensils, surfaces, oil or hands. Cleaning methods must remove allergen protein.

Anaphylaxis: call 999 and say 'anaphylaxis'; help use the person's own adrenaline auto-injector. Based on NHS and Resuscitation Council UK advice (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/anaphylaxis/). Simplified; first-aid steps beyond this are for a first aid course.
Not verified: any penalty figures. None are stated in the session on purpose.

Review Oct 2026: 14 allergens, the 10 mg per kg or litre sulphite threshold and PPDS / Natasha's Law (1 October 2021) confirmed. Non-prepacked food: the legal minimum is still that information must be available, by any means including orally with clear signposting; the FSA published best-practice guidance in March 2025 recommending written information for every dish, backed by a conversation, and the slide now says which is which. The FSA evaluation of that guidance (due spring 2026) could lead to mandatory written information ('Owen's Law'); GM/Ward Hadaway to check whether that has happened. Loose drinks (draught beer, wine by the glass, cocktails) count as non-prepacked food for allergen information. Anaphylaxis: NHS advice also says to lay the person flat with legs raised (sit up if breathing is difficult); the slide says 'calm and still' and leaves detail to first aid training.

cards.kicker: Kitchen, front of house and bar · 15 minutes
cards.title: Allergen awareness
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- name the 14 allergens and explain cross-contact
- take and pass on an allergy order without any guesswork
- recognise anaphylaxis and know what to do

cards.title: The 14 allergens
cards.body: By law, 14 allergens must be declared. Guests can be seriously harmed by tiny amounts, and cooking does not remove them.

items: Cereals containing gluten (wheat, rye, barley, oats)

cards.title: Which foods hide them
cards.body: Allergens turn up in sauces, stock, dressings and garnishes. Sulphites count when over 10 mg per kg or per litre, as in some wines and dried fruit. Tree nuts means named ones like almonds and cashews, and peanuts are separate. If you are not sure what is in something, you do not know it is safe.

items.title: Sauces and stock
items.text: Celery, mustard, gluten and milk are common

items.title: Drinks
items.text: Wine and beer can contain sulphites or gluten

items.title: Garnishes
items.text: A sprinkle of nuts or seeds counts

cards.title: What cross-contact is
cards.body: Cross-contact is when an allergen gets into food that does not contain it. A trace is enough to cause a reaction. A wipe does not always remove it, so clean thoroughly.

items.title: Utensils and boards
items.text: Same knife or board used for different foods

items.title: Fryer oil
items.text: Battered fish and chips in shared oil

cards.title: From the guest to the kitchen
cards.body: Never guess, never assume, never say 'it should be fine'. If you do not know, ask the kitchen. Your manager will show you how allergy orders are flagged and who the allergen lead is.

items.title: Check
items.text: Look in the allergen matrix or ask the chef

items.title: Flag
items.text: Mark the order clearly, tell the kitchen in person

items.title: Serve
items.text: Hand over with the allergy order, tell the guest

cards.title: Information for every dish
cards.body:
Guests must be able to find allergen information for every dish and drink we serve. By law it can be given by word of mouth if there is a clear sign telling guests to ask, but the FSA's best practice is to have it written down and easy to find, backed up by a conversation. Your manager will show you where the allergen matrix is kept.

Pre-packed for direct sale food (PPDS), such as a sandwich wrapped on site, needs a full ingredients label with allergens emphasised. This is Natasha's Law, in force from 1 October 2021.

right.title: Never
items: Pick off the allergen and serve

cards.title: Anaphylaxis: act at once
cards.body: A severe reaction can start within minutes. Signs include swelling of the lips, face, tongue or throat, difficulty breathing or wheezing, a rash or hives, feeling faint, and collapse. **Call 999** and say 'anaphylaxis'. If the guest has their own adrenaline auto-injector, help them use it. Do not leave them alone, and tell a manager.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Know the 14 allergens. Cooking does not remove them.
- Cross-contact: even a trace on a board, glove, pan or fryer oil can cause a reaction.
- Never guess or say 'it should be fine'. Check the matrix or ask the chef.
- Every dish needs allergen information guests can get.
- Suspected anaphylaxis: call 999 straight away.

cards.q: A guest says she is allergic to nuts and asks if the pudding is safe. You think it has none. What do you do?
options: Say it should be fine and serve it as it is
Check the matrix and ask the chef before answering
Tell her to just leave the garnish off the plate
Ask her to look at the menu and decide herself
cards.why: Never answer from memory. Recipes change, so check the matrix or ask the kitchen before giving any answer.

cards.q: Cooking food at a high temperature removes allergens.
cards.why: Allergens are proteins that survive cooking. Only leaving the allergen out, and avoiding cross-contact, makes a dish safe.

options: Using the same tongs for prawns, then a veggie plate
Serving a guest a dish they said they cannot eat
Forgetting to ask the table about allergies
Leaving a finished dish on the pass for too long
cards.why: Cross-contact is an allergen transferring to food that does not contain it, such as via shared tongs, boards, oil or hands.

cards.q: Which TWO are among the 14 allergens?
options: Garlic
Sesame
Lupin
Tomato
Chilli
cards.why: Sesame and lupin are both on the list of 14. Garlic, tomato and chilli are not.

cards.q: A guest starts wheezing, their lips swell and they feel faint after eating. What is the first thing to do?
options: Give them water and wait to see if it passes
Take them outside to get some fresh air
Call 999, say anaphylaxis, stay with them
Offer them antihistamines from the first aid kit
cards.why: These are signs of anaphylaxis, a medical emergency. Call 999 and stay with them while you help use their own auto-injector.

cards.q: Wheat, rye, barley and oats all count as cereals containing gluten.
cards.why: Cereals containing gluten is one of the 14 allergens and includes wheat, rye, barley and oats.

cards.q: A guest asks what is in the sauce and the chef is busy. What do you do?
options: Tell them it is only stock and cream
Say it is probably free of what they mentioned
Look in the matrix or wait for the chef
Pick a different dish for them without checking
cards.why: Never answer from memory or guess. Use the allergen matrix, or wait for the chef to confirm.

cards.q: Which of these is pre-packed for direct sale, so needs a full ingredients label with allergens emphasised?
options: A steak cooked to order and sent to a table
A cocktail mixed and poured at the bar for a guest
A plated starter carried out to a wedding table
A sandwich wrapped earlier and left in the chiller to grab
cards.why: Food packed on the premises before the guest orders it is PPDS. Natasha's Law has required full labels since 1 October 2021.

cards.q: Which of these could be a sign of a severe allergic reaction?
options: Sneezing after the pepper mill
Swelling of the lips or tongue
A flushed face from a warm room
Feeling full after the main course
cards.why: Swelling of the lips, face, tongue or throat is a warning sign of anaphylaxis, along with breathing difficulty and feeling faint.

cards.q: Which TWO must you never do when a guest tells you about an allergy?
options: Tell the kitchen in person
Say it should be fine
Check the matrix
Remove the nuts from the dish and serve it
Mark the order clearly
cards.why: Picking an allergen off a dish leaves traces behind, and 'it should be fine' is a guess. Check, flag and tell the kitchen.
